section_title: What does Solomon ask when sin brings defeat or distress?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 33 When Your people Israel are defeated before an enemy because they have sinned against You, and they return to You and confess Your name, praying and pleading with You in this temple, 34 then may You hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your people Israel. May You restore them to the land You gave to their fathers. 35 When the skies are shut and there is no rain because Your people have sinned against You, and they pray toward this place and confess Your name, and they turn from their sins because You have afflicted them, 36 then may You hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your servants, Your people Israel, so that You may teach them the good way in which they should walk. May You send rain on the land that You gave Your people as an inheritance.

37 When famine or plague comes upon the land, or blight or mildew or locusts or grasshoppers, or when their enemy besieges them in their cities, whatever plague or sickness may come, 38 then may whatever prayer or petition Your people Israel make—each knowing his own afflictions and spreading out his hands toward this temple— 39 be heard by You from heaven, Your dwelling place. And may You forgive and act, and repay each man according to all his ways, since You know his heart—for You alone know the hearts of all men— 40 so that they may fear You all the days they live in the land that You gave to our fathers.

context_lines: Solomon next prays about defeat by enemies and a lack of rain because Israel has sinned against the LORD. He asks that when the people turn back, confess and pray, God will forgive, restore and teach them how to live.

These requests fit the warnings given to Israel in [Leviticus 26:14–20](https://biblehub.com/bsb/leviticus/26.htm), where breaking the covenant brings defeat and failing harvests. The prayer also reaches into famine, disease, crop damage and siege, including the afflictions known to each person.
God alone knows every heart. Solomon asks Him to hear, forgive and act with that complete knowledge, so the people will live in reverence for Him.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-kings/) highlights the order of the request: forgiveness and learning the right way come before the plea for rain. The need is deeper than relief from the immediate hardship.

[Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_kings/8.htm) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/8.htm) take the language about the heart’s affliction as an invitation to recognize and confess inward sin. Gill also notes the parallel wording in Chronicles about a person’s own grief and trouble.

The stated setting is Israel’s covenant life in the land. The passage calls for honest repentance and trust in God’s knowledge of the heart. It does not give readers the knowledge to identify a particular sin behind every other person’s illness or hardship.
god_plan_lines: A broader theme comes into view in [Hebrews 12:5–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/12.htm): God’s correction is directed toward the good of His children, so that they share in His holiness and learn to live rightly. The settings differ, but in both, the purpose reaches beyond ending the pain.

[1 John 1:7–9](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_john/1.htm) also connects honest acknowledgment of sin with forgiveness and cleansing through Jesus. Together these passages show why turning to God involves more than asking circumstances to improve. It includes receiving His mercy and learning His ways.
